summary: How the kidneys, ureters, and bladder develop from intermediate mesoderm and the cloaca. Exam questions take one developmental step and ask what goes wrong when it fails: renal agenesis, horseshoe kidney, duplex ureter, urachal remnants, and posterior urethral valves.

points: All three come from intermediate mesoderm and appear in order from head to tail.
Pronephros: week 4, in the neck region, never works, and regresses.
Mesonephros: appears in week 4 as the pronephros regresses, works briefly as an interim kidney in the first trimester; its duct (mesonephric or Wolffian duct) persists in males as genital ducts.
Metanephros: appears in week 5 and becomes the permanent kidney; it starts making urine late in the first trimester, and that urine becomes most of the amniotic fluid later in pregnancy.
notes.why: All three kidneys arise from intermediate mesoderm in a head to tail sequence, and the mesonephric duct links them: its outgrowth, the ureteric bud, starts the permanent kidney, and in males the duct itself becomes the ductus deferens and related ducts. The metanephros begins producing urine at about weeks 10 to 12, and from the second trimester on, fetal urine is the main source of amniotic fluid. That link explains why anything that stops fetal urine output, from bilateral renal agenesis to outlet obstruction, shows up as oligohydramnios.

points: The ureteric bud grows out of the mesonephric duct and pushes into the metanephric mesenchyme (metanephric blastema).
The bud tells the mesenchyme to form nephrons; the mesenchyme tells the bud to branch (GDNF from mesenchyme acts on the RET receptor of the bud).
Ureteric bud forms the collecting system: collecting ducts, minor and major calyces, renal pelvis, ureter.
Metanephric mesenchyme forms the nephron: Bowman capsule, proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule.
If the bud never reaches the mesenchyme, no kidney forms (renal agenesis). Bilateral agenesis causes oligohydramnios and Potter sequence (pulmonary hypoplasia, flat face, limb deformities).
The ureteropelvic junction is the last part to canalize, so it is the most common site of congenital obstruction and hydronephrosis.
notes.why: Neither tissue can build a kidney alone. GDNF from the metanephric mesenchyme binds RET on the ureteric bud and drives branching, and each new bud tip signals the surrounding mesenchyme to condense and turn into an epithelial nephron. A defect in either partner, or a bud that never arrives, ends with no nephrons at all. Bilateral agenesis means no fetal urine, so oligohydramnios follows, and the compressed fetus with underdeveloped lungs shows Potter sequence.

points: The kidneys form in the pelvis and ascend to the lumbar region, picking up new arteries from the aorta as they rise; lower ones normally regress.
Persistent lower vessels become accessory renal arteries; failed ascent leaves a pelvic kidney.
Horseshoe kidney: the lower poles fuse, and the fused isthmus catches under the inferior mesenteric artery, so the kidneys stay low.
Horseshoe kidney is often silent but raises the risk of ureteropelvic obstruction, hydronephrosis, stones, and infection; it is linked to Turner syndrome.
notes.why: The kidneys rise mostly because the lumbar and sacral body grows away below them, and at each level they take new arterial branches from the aorta while the lower ones normally regress. A lower branch that persists becomes an accessory renal artery, which is an end artery to its part of the kidney. When the lower poles fuse, the isthmus catches under the root of the inferior mesenteric artery and ascent stops. The fused kidney is also malrotated, with ureters that cross over the isthmus, which explains its higher rates of ureteropelvic obstruction, stasis, stones, and infection.

points: Early splitting of one bud gives a bifid (partial) ureter that joins before the bladder.
Two separate buds give a complete duplex ureter with two orifices.
In complete duplication the upper pole ureter opens lower and more medial and tends to obstruct (often with a ureterocele); the lower pole ureter opens higher and lateral and tends to reflux.
In a girl, an ectopic ureter that opens below the urethral sphincter (urethra or vagina) causes constant dribbling despite normal voiding.
notes.why: A single bud that divides early gives two ureters that merge before the bladder, while two buds from the mesonephric duct give two complete ureters with separate orifices. In complete duplication the Weigert-Meyer rule applies: the lower pole ureter is absorbed into the bladder first and carried upward and laterally, so its intramural tunnel is short and it refluxes. The upper pole ureter stays with the mesonephric duct longer, so it ends lower and more medially, where it is prone to ectopia, ureterocele, and obstruction. In a girl, an ectopic orifice below the external sphincter bypasses continence entirely.

points: The urorectal septum divides the cloaca into the urogenital sinus in front and the anorectal canal behind (done by about week 7).
The urogenital sinus forms the bladder and urethra. The trigone comes from the incorporated mesonephric ducts.
The allantois connects the bladder apex to the umbilicus and normally closes into the urachus, then the median umbilical ligament.
Patent urachus: urine leaks from the umbilicus. Urachal cyst: a closed pocket that can become infected. Urachal remnants carry a risk of adenocarcinoma.
notes.why: The urorectal septum grows toward the cloacal membrane and divides the cloaca into front and back chambers, so errors in this step leave fistulas between the urinary tract and the rectum. As the bladder enlarges, the caudal mesonephric ducts are absorbed into its back wall to form the trigone, which places the ureteric orifices at its upper corners. The allantois must fibrose into the urachus; if it stays fully open, urine leaks at the umbilicus, and if only a middle segment stays open, it forms a cyst. Remnants are lined by glandular epithelium, which is why their cancers are adenocarcinomas.

points: Membrane-like folds in the posterior (prostatic) urethra of male infants block outflow.
Backpressure gives a thick-walled, distended bladder and bilateral hydronephrosis.
Low fetal urine output causes oligohydramnios and can lead to pulmonary hypoplasia.
notes.why: The valves sit below the bladder, so the entire urinary tract above them is under high pressure. The detrusor thickens as it pushes against the blocked outlet, and backpressure travels up both ureters, giving bilateral hydroureteronephrosis that can permanently damage the developing kidneys. Because fetal urine supplies most amniotic fluid in the second half of pregnancy, low output causes oligohydramnios, and too little fluid limits fetal breathing movements and lung growth, producing pulmonary hypoplasia.

tricks.label: Bud builds the plumbing
tricks.text: The ureteric bud makes everything that carries finished urine (collecting ducts to ureter). The mesenchyme makes everything that makes urine (capsule to distal tubule).

tricks.label: Pro, meso, meta
tricks.text: The Greek prefixes mean first, middle, and after. Only the after kidney (metanephros, week 5) stays.

tricks.text: In a duplex system the upper pole ureter enters the bladder lower and obstructs; the lower pole ureter enters higher and refluxes. The two cross.

highYield: Metanephros appears in week 5 and becomes the permanent kidney.
Bilateral renal agenesis means no fetal urine, oligohydramnios, and Potter sequence with pulmonary hypoplasia.
The ureteropelvic junction is the most common site of congenital urinary obstruction.
Horseshoe kidney is trapped below the inferior mesenteric artery and is linked to Turner syndrome.
Fluid leaking from a newborn's umbilicus that is urine means a patent urachus.
Posterior urethral valves are the classic cause of bladder outlet obstruction in a male newborn.
Constant dribbling with normal voiding in a girl suggests an ectopic ureter below the sphincter.
pitfalls: Collecting ducts come from the ureteric bud, while the distal convoluted tubule comes from mesenchyme. The dividing line is between the distal tubule and the collecting duct.
The artery that traps a horseshoe kidney is the inferior mesenteric artery; the superior mesenteric artery arises higher and is out of the way.

When a fetal anomaly is the cause, oligohydramnios points to a fetal urine problem (agenesis, valves) and polyhydramnios points to a swallowing or gut problem. Ruptured membranes are the other common cause of oligohydramnios.
A patent urachus drains urine; a patent vitelline duct drains meconium or bowel contents from the umbilicus.

summary: The microscopic structure of the nephron, the juxtaglomerular apparatus, and the bladder wall. Exam questions link structure to function: the filtration barrier to proteinuria, tubule cell type to job and to ischemic injury, loop length to concentrating ability, and urothelium to a stretchy, watertight lining.

points: Layer 1, fenestrated endothelium: pores hold back blood cells.
Layer 2, glomerular basement membrane: type IV collagen and laminin, with heparan sulfate giving a strong negative charge.
Layer 3, podocyte foot processes: the slit diaphragm between them (nephrin) is the final size filter.
The barrier filters by size and by charge; albumin is negatively charged and is repelled.
Loss of the negative charge or effacement of foot processes lets albumin through (selective albuminuria, as in minimal change disease).
notes.why: Each layer adds a different barrier, so the filter selects by size and by charge at once. Albumin is small enough to enter the wall but carries a net negative charge, so the heparan sulfate of the basement membrane repels it, and the nephrin slit diaphragm stops what gets past. In minimal change disease, foot process effacement and loss of the negative charge let albumin through while larger globulins are still held back, so the proteinuria is selective. Structural damage to the basement membrane or capillary wall lets larger proteins through as well, giving nonselective proteinuria.

points: Juxtaglomerular cells: modified smooth muscle in the afferent arteriole wall that store and secrete renin.
Macula densa: tall, crowded cells at the end of the thick ascending limb where it touches its own glomerulus; they sense tubular NaCl.
Extraglomerular mesangial (lacis) cells sit between the afferent and efferent arterioles and the macula densa.
Intraglomerular mesangial cells support the capillary loops, contract, make matrix, and phagocytose trapped proteins and immune complexes.
notes.why: The juxtaglomerular apparatus sits where each nephron's thick ascending limb returns to touch its own glomerulus, which lets the kidney match filtration to what the tubule is receiving. Macula densa cells sense luminal NaCl through NKCC2: high NaCl constricts the afferent arteriole through adenosine (tubuloglomerular feedback), and low NaCl signals the juxtaglomerular cells to release renin through prostaglandins and nitric oxide. Mesangial cells are smooth muscle-like cells whose contraction adjusts filtering surface area, and their job of clearing trapped proteins places them in the path of circulating immune complexes, which is where IgA deposits in IgA nephropathy.

points: Proximal tubule: simple cuboidal with a tall brush border (microvilli), many mitochondria, basal infoldings, and pink cytoplasm.
Thin limbs: simple squamous; the descending thin limb is permeable to water.
Thick ascending limb and distal tubule: cuboidal with no brush border, so the lumen looks wider and cleaner.
Collecting duct: cuboidal to columnar with clear cell borders; principal cells handle Na+, K+, and water, intercalated cells handle acid and bicarbonate.
The proximal tubule straight part and the medullary thick ascending limb use the most ATP and get the least oxygen, so they die first in ischemic acute tubular necrosis.
notes.why: Cell structure follows workload. The proximal tubule moves most filtered solute, so it needs a huge apical surface (the brush border) and dense mitochondria packed into basal infoldings to power the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase that drives nearly all its transport. The thick ascending limb is also mitochondria-rich, and both the proximal straight tubule and the medullary thick ascending limb sit in the outer medulla, where oxygen is scarce because little blood flows there. High ATP demand with low oxygen supply makes these segments fail first in ischemia, and their shed cells form muddy brown granular casts.

points: Cortical nephrons (most nephrons): glomeruli in the outer cortex, short loops that barely enter the medulla, peritubular capillaries.
Juxtamedullary nephrons: glomeruli near the corticomedullary junction, long loops deep into the inner medulla, efferent arterioles that form the vasa recta.
Long loops build the steep medullary osmotic gradient, so juxtamedullary nephrons drive urine concentration.
notes.why: Loop length sets how much osmolality the loop can build along the corticomedullary axis, because countercurrent multiplication adds a small increment at each level. Only the long loops of juxtamedullary nephrons reach the inner medulla, and their efferent arterioles form the vasa recta that preserve the gradient. This is why desert rodents, with relatively more long loops and a thick medulla, concentrate urine far better than humans, and why damage confined to the medulla, as in sickle cell nephropathy, causes an early loss of concentrating ability.

points: Urothelium (transitional epithelium) lines the calyces, pelvis, ureters, bladder, and upper urethra.
Surface umbrella cells are large, sometimes binucleate, and carry stiff uroplakin plaques on their apical membrane.
Tight junctions and uroplakin plaques make the lining impermeable to urine.
On filling, the cells flatten and stored membrane vesicles fuse with the surface, so the lining stretches without tearing.
Under the urothelium: lamina propria, then the detrusor muscle in interwoven smooth muscle layers, then adventitia (serosa over the dome).
notes.why: Urine can differ greatly from plasma in osmolality, pH, and urea concentration, so the urothelium must be a near-perfect barrier. Uroplakin proteins assemble into rigid plaques across the apical membrane of umbrella cells, and tight junctions seal the spaces between cells, so neither water nor solutes cross readily. During filling, the cells flatten and fusiform vesicles holding preformed uroplakin plaques insert into the surface membrane, adding area without breaking the seal. The interwoven detrusor bundles squeeze the lumen from all directions, which lets the bladder empty from any filling volume.

tricks.text: A brush border plus packed mitochondria means a hard-working absorber (proximal tubule), and hard workers are the first to die when oxygen runs out.

Vasa recta come from efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons; cortical nephrons feed peritubular capillaries.

summary: Where the kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra sit, what touches them, and how they are wrapped. Exam questions use these relations to predict where stones lodge, which organ is hurt in trauma, and why women get more bladder infections.

points: The kidneys are retroperitoneal, lying beside the vertebral column from about T12 to L3.
The right kidney sits a little lower than the left because the liver sits above it.
The hilum faces medially at about L1; the suprarenal glands cap the upper poles.
Posterior relations: diaphragm and 12th rib above, psoas major medially, quadratus lumborum behind, transversus abdominis laterally.
The subcostal, iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves run behind the kidney.
notes.why: The kidneys lie in the paravertebral gutters of the posterior abdominal wall, so their posterior relations are the muscles of that wall and the diaphragm above. The large right lobe of the liver pushes the right kidney slightly lower than the left. Because the upper pole lies against the diaphragm, the kidney moves a few centimeters with breathing, and the pleural recess reaches below the 12th rib medially, so a high posterior approach can enter the pleural cavity. The subcostal, iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves crossing behind the kidney explain why a renal or perinephric process can refer pain to the lower abdominal wall and groin.

points: Right kidney: liver, descending (second part) duodenum, right colic flexure.
Left kidney: stomach, spleen, tail of the pancreas, jejunum, left colic flexure.
The descending duodenum lies directly on the right hilum, so right renal procedures can injure it.
notes.why: The duodenum, pancreas, and colic flexures are secondarily retroperitoneal, so they lie directly on the kidney with no peritoneum in between, while the liver, stomach, spleen, and jejunum are separated from it by peritoneum. Direct contact explains why right renal surgery or a right renal mass can injure or invade the descending duodenum. On the left, the spleen lies against the upper lateral kidney, so blunt left flank trauma often injures the spleen and left kidney together.

points: From inside out: fibrous capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia, pararenal fat.
Renal fascia encloses the kidney, perirenal fat, and suprarenal gland.
At the hilum, front to back: renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis.
notes.why: The coverings form compartments. The renal (Gerota) fascia wraps the kidney, perirenal fat, and suprarenal gland, so blood or pus from the kidney stays in the perirenal space at first and can push the kidney out of position. Perirenal fat helps hold the kidney in place, so rapid fat loss can let the kidney drop (nephroptosis). The hilar order is fixed from front to back as vein, artery, pelvis, so on a posterior surgical approach the pelvis is reached first and the vein last.

points: Each ureter (about 25 cm) runs down on the psoas major, behind the gonadal vessels.
It crosses the common iliac bifurcation (or start of the external iliac) at the pelvic brim.
It enters the bladder wall obliquely, which acts as a flap valve against reflux.
Stones lodge at the three narrow points: ureteropelvic junction, pelvic brim, ureterovesical junction (the narrowest).
notes.why: Peristalsis pushes urine down the ureter, but a stone moves only as far as the lumen allows, so it stops where the tube narrows or bends. The ureteropelvic junction narrows as the funnel-shaped pelvis tapers, the pelvic brim is where the ureter angles over the iliac vessels, and the ureterovesical junction is narrowest because the ureter runs obliquely through the muscular bladder wall. That oblique tunnel is squeezed shut as bladder pressure rises, which normally prevents reflux; a short tunnel allows vesicoureteral reflux and predisposes to pyelonephritis.

points: Trigone: smooth triangle between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice.
Male urethra (about 18 to 22 cm): prostatic, membranous (through the external sphincter, narrowest), spongy (bulbous part then penile part).
Female urethra is about 4 cm and opens just in front of the vagina, so bacteria from the perineum reach the bladder easily.
notes.why: The trigone is smooth because its mucosa is firmly bound to the underlying muscle, while the rest of the bladder lining folds into rugae when empty. In men the urethra runs through the prostate and then the external sphincter, so prostatic enlargement narrows the prostatic part, and the membranous part is the fixed, least distensible segment. The female urethra is short and opens near the vaginal introitus and anus, so bowel flora such as Escherichia coli that colonize the periurethral area travel only about 4 cm to reach the bladder, which is why women have far more cystitis.

points: Pelvic fracture tears the posterior urethra at the membranous segment: blood at the meatus, high-riding prostate, urine into the retropubic space.
Straddle injury crushes the bulbous spongy urethra against the pubis below the perineal membrane.
If Buck fascia tears, urine fills the superficial perineal space and spreads into the scrotum, penis, and lower anterior abdominal wall, but not the thighs.
notes.why: The perineal membrane anchors the membranous urethra to the pubic arch, so when a pelvic fracture displaces the prostate, the urethra tears at that fixed point and the freed prostate rides high on rectal exam. A straddle injury instead crushes the bulbous urethra against the pubic arch below the membrane. If Buck fascia holds, the urine stays along the penis; if it tears, urine enters the superficial perineal space bounded by Colles fascia. That fascia continues into the scrotum, penis, and Scarpa fascia of the abdominal wall, but it fuses with the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament, so urine never reaches the thighs.

summary: How the urinary organs relate to the peritoneum and the pelvis. Exam questions use these relations to explain bladder rupture patterns, where pain is felt, why the ureter is hit during hysterectomy, and what kind of incontinence a patient has.

points: Kidneys and ureters are retroperitoneal on the posterior abdominal wall.
The bladder is extraperitoneal in the pelvis; only its superior surface (dome) is covered by peritoneum.
A full bladder rises above the pubis and lifts peritoneum off the anterior abdominal wall.
notes.why: The kidneys and ureters develop and stay behind the parietal peritoneum, while the bladder sits below it in the pelvis with peritoneum draped only over its superior surface. As the bladder fills, it rises into the extraperitoneal space behind the anterior abdominal wall and peels the peritoneum upward. That is why a distended bladder can be entered by a suprapubic needle or catheter just above the pubic symphysis without entering the peritoneal cavity.

points: Blunt blow to a full bladder (seat belt, a blow while intoxicated) bursts the dome, the weakest part.
Dome rupture is intraperitoneal: urine fills the peritoneal cavity and causes ascites and peritonitis.
Pelvic fracture fragments tear the anterolateral wall low down, so urine leaks extraperitoneally into the retropubic space.
notes.why: Where the bladder tears decides where urine goes. A full bladder is a thin-walled sphere under tension, and a sudden pressure rise bursts it at the dome, the least supported part and the only part covered by peritoneum, so urine pours into the peritoneal cavity. The peritoneum then absorbs urea and creatinine from the spilled urine, so serum levels can rise without true kidney injury. A pelvic fracture instead lacerates the low anterolateral wall below the peritoneum, so urine collects in the retropubic space and stays extraperitoneal.

points: Male: peritoneum runs from the bladder dome straight onto the rectum, forming the rectovesical pouch.
Female: peritoneum runs from the bladder onto the uterus (vesicouterine pouch), then from the uterus onto the rectum (rectouterine pouch).
The rectovesical pouch in men and the rectouterine pouch in women are the lowest points of the peritoneal cavity, where fluid pools when upright.
notes.why: Peritoneum drapes over whatever pelvic organs lie in its path, so a pouch forms wherever it dips between two organs. In men nothing lies between the bladder and rectum, giving a single rectovesical pouch; in women the uterus sits in between and splits the space into a shallow vesicouterine pouch in front and a deep rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) behind. Because these are the lowest points of the peritoneal cavity when upright, blood, pus, or tumor cells collect there, and the rectouterine pouch can be reached through the posterior vaginal fornix.

points: Visceral pain fibers from the kidney and ureter travel with sympathetic nerves into roughly the T11 to L2 cord segments.
The brain reads the pain in the skin served by those segments: flank, groin, scrotum or labia, and upper anterior thigh.
As a stone moves down, the pain moves from flank toward groin.
Costovertebral angle (12th rib meets the erector spinae): the kidney lies right under it, so tapping there hurts in pyelonephritis.
Perinephric pus stays inside the renal fascia, but the fascia is open below, so pus can track down toward the pelvis.
notes.why: Visceral afferents from the kidney and ureter run with sympathetic fibers into about T11 to L2, the segments that also receive skin input from the flank, groin, genitalia, and upper anterior thigh. Both inputs converge on the same dorsal horn neurons, so the brain refers the visceral pain to that skin, and the pain moves groinward as the stone descends. Percussion at the costovertebral angle jars an inflamed kidney with a stretched capsule. The renal fascia holds perinephric pus around the kidney but is loosely closed below, so pus can track toward the pelvis.

points: Near the cervix the ureter passes under the uterine artery, about 1 to 2 cm lateral to the cervix.
Clamping the uterine artery at hysterectomy can catch the ureter.
Ligation blocks drainage and causes hydronephrosis with flank pain; transection leaks urine (urinoma or a fistula with constant vaginal leakage).
The ureter is also at risk at the pelvic brim, where it lies next to the ovarian vessels.
notes.why: Near the cervix, the uterine artery runs medially in the base of the broad ligament and crosses above and in front of the ureter, which passes underneath on its way to the bladder (water under the bridge). A clamp or ligature placed on the uterine artery close to that crossing can include the ureter. Ligation blocks drainage, so the kidney above dilates and the patient has flank pain, while a cut ureter leaks urine into the pelvis or opens a fistula into the vagina. At the pelvic brim the ureter lies close to the ovarian vessels, so ligating those vessels during oophorectomy also puts it at risk.

points: Stress: weak pelvic floor or urethral support lets urine leak when abdominal pressure rises (cough, laugh, lift); risk rises after vaginal delivery and menopause.
Cystocele: the bladder bulges into the anterior vaginal wall when its support weakens.
Urge: involuntary detrusor contractions (detrusor overactivity) give a sudden need to void and leakage on the way.
Overflow: the bladder cannot empty (weak detrusor or outlet blockage), so it overfills and dribbles; post-void residual is high.
notes.why: Continence requires urethral closure pressure to exceed bladder pressure at all times. In stress incontinence, weak pelvic floor and urethral support (after vaginal delivery, or with estrogen loss at menopause) let the urethra sag, so a cough raises bladder pressure without compressing the urethra equally. In urge incontinence, uninhibited detrusor contractions push bladder pressure above urethral pressure without warning. In overflow incontinence, bladder pressure exceeds urethral resistance only when the bladder is overfilled, because the detrusor is weak (diabetic neuropathy, sacral cord lesion) or the outlet is blocked (prostatic enlargement).

summary: How blood flows through the kidney and how arteriole tone sets filtration. Exam questions ask you to predict GFR and filtration fraction after drugs or disease change the arterioles, and to link vascular anatomy to infarcts, papillary necrosis, and a left varicocele.

points: Renal artery, segmental arteries, interlobar arteries (between pyramids), arcuate arteries (at the corticomedullary junction), cortical radiate arteries.
Then afferent arteriole, glomerular capillaries, efferent arteriole.
Efferent arterioles of cortical nephrons form peritubular capillaries; those of juxtamedullary nephrons form the vasa recta.
Veins run back the same way to the renal vein.
The kidneys get about 20 to 25 percent of cardiac output.
notes.why: Blood passes through two capillary beds in series, and this arrangement is the basis of renal function. The glomerular bed is a high-pressure bed held between two resistance vessels, so filtration can be adjusted at either end. The peritubular bed downstream is low in pressure and high in oncotic pressure, because filtration has concentrated the plasma proteins, and both features favor reabsorption. The kidneys receive about a fifth of cardiac output because their job is to process plasma, far more than their oxygen needs require.

points: Segmental and interlobar arteries do not connect with each other, so each one is the only supply to its territory.
Blocking one (usually an embolus from the left heart, as in atrial fibrillation) kills a wedge of tissue.
Renal infarcts are pale (ischemic), wedge-shaped, with the base at the capsule and the tip pointing to the medulla.
notes.why: Segmental and interlobar arteries have no useful connections with their neighbors, so the tissue each one supplies has no backup route. An embolus, most often thrombus from the left atrium or left ventricle, lodges and causes coagulative necrosis in a cone that matches the branching pattern, with the base at the capsule and the apex toward the medulla. Solid organs with a single blood supply, such as the kidney, form pale infarcts, unlike the hemorrhagic infarcts of dual-supply organs such as the lung. A thin rim of outer cortex can survive because capsular vessels supply it.

points: Afferent constriction lowers both renal plasma flow (RPF) and GFR; filtration fraction (GFR/RPF) stays about the same.
Efferent constriction raises glomerular pressure, so GFR rises while RPF falls; filtration fraction rises.
Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole; NSAIDs remove that and drop GFR in a volume-depleted patient.
Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole more; ACE inhibitors remove that and drop GFR in bilateral renal artery stenosis.
notes.why: Glomerular capillary pressure sits between the afferent and efferent resistances, so changing either one changes GFR. Constricting the afferent arteriole lowers both glomerular pressure and flow, so GFR and RPF fall together. Constricting the efferent arteriole backs pressure up into the glomerulus, raising GFR while total flow falls, so filtration fraction rises. When renal perfusion is low, the kidney relies on prostaglandin afferent dilation and angiotensin II efferent constriction to hold GFR, which is why NSAIDs or ACE inhibitors can cause acute kidney injury in that setting.

points: Renal blood flow and GFR stay nearly constant over a mean arterial pressure range of roughly 80 to 180 mm Hg.
Myogenic response: higher pressure stretches the afferent arteriole wall, which contracts back.
Tubuloglomerular feedback: higher GFR sends more NaCl to the macula densa, which releases adenosine and constricts the afferent arteriole.
Low NaCl at the macula densa does the reverse: afferent dilation plus renin release.
notes.why: Autoregulation keeps GFR steady so normal swings in blood pressure do not flood or starve the tubules. The myogenic response belongs to the vessel itself: stretch opens cation channels in afferent smooth muscle, the cell depolarizes, calcium enters, and the arteriole constricts within seconds. Tubuloglomerular feedback senses the result: more NaCl reaching the macula densa leads to ATP and adenosine release, and adenosine acting on A1 receptors constricts the afferent arteriole to bring GFR back down. Below the autoregulatory range, flow follows pressure directly, which is why shock lowers GFR.

points: Vasa recta run in hairpin loops beside the loops of Henle and carry only about 1 to 2 percent of renal blood flow.
Slow flow and countercurrent exchange carry away reabsorbed water without washing out the medullary salt and urea.
Oxygen shunts across from descending to ascending vessels, so the inner medulla is hypoxic as well as hypertonic.
Low oxygen and high osmolality make HbS red cells sickle in the vasa recta, causing papillary necrosis, hematuria, and loss of concentrating ability, even in sickle cell trait.
notes.why: The vasa recta act as a countercurrent exchanger: descending blood picks up solute and loses water as it enters the hypertonic medulla, and ascending blood gives the solute back and regains water on its way to the cortex. Exchange is passive, so it keeps the gradient only if flow is slow; high medullary blood flow washes out solute and weakens concentrating ability. The same exchange shunts oxygen from descending to ascending vessels and leaves the papilla hypoxic. In that hypoxic, hypertonic, slow-flowing setting, HbS polymerizes, red cells sickle and block the vessels, and the papillary tip infarcts.

points: The left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta, just below the superior mesenteric artery, to reach the IVC.
The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein; the right gonadal vein drains straight into the IVC.
Renal cell carcinoma growing into the left renal vein blocks left gonadal drainage and causes a left varicocele that stays when the patient lies down.
Compression of the left renal vein between the aorta and superior mesenteric artery (nutcracker) can also cause hematuria and a left varicocele.
notes.why: The left renal vein is longer than the right because it must cross the midline to reach the IVC, and on the way it passes through the angle between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery. It also receives the left gonadal and left suprarenal veins, so anything that raises its pressure backs up into the left testicular vein and pampiniform plexus. Renal cell carcinoma tends to grow into the renal vein, and the varicocele it causes does not empty when the patient lies down, unlike a common idiopathic varicocele, which does.

summary: How the kidney filters plasma, reclaims what the body needs, secretes waste, concentrates urine, and empties the bladder. This is the most calculation-heavy unit: expect to work clearance numbers, predict GFR changes, sort out hyponatremia and polyuria, and place a neurologic lesion from the bladder pattern.

points: Net filtration pressure = glomerular capillary pressure (about 60 mm Hg) minus Bowman space pressure (about 18) minus glomerular oncotic pressure (about 32).
GFR = Kf times net filtration pressure; normal GFR is about 125 mL/min.
Ureteral obstruction raises Bowman space pressure and lowers GFR.
Hypoalbuminemia lowers plasma oncotic pressure and tends to raise GFR.
Dehydration concentrates plasma proteins (higher oncotic pressure) and lowers renal flow, so GFR falls.
notes.why: Filtration depends on the balance of pressures across the glomerular capillary wall, and each condition shifts one term. Glomerular hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out, while Bowman space pressure and plasma oncotic pressure push back. Obstruction raises the pressure in Bowman space, low albumin removes some of the oncotic opposition, and dehydration both concentrates proteins and lowers renal flow. Because filtration removes protein-free fluid, oncotic pressure rises along the capillary, and higher plasma flow raises GFR by keeping that rise smaller.

points: Clearance = (urine concentration times urine flow) / plasma concentration.
Inulin is filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals GFR. Creatinine slightly overestimates GFR because a little is secreted.
PAH is filtered and secreted almost completely, so its clearance is effective renal plasma flow (about 650 mL/min).
Filtration fraction = GFR / RPF, normally about 20 percent.
Clearance below GFR means net reabsorption (glucose, urea); above GFR means net secretion (PAH).
notes.why: Clearance is the volume of plasma that would have to be fully cleared of a substance each minute to account for the amount appearing in urine. Inulin is handled only by filtration, so the volume cleared equals the volume filtered, which is GFR. PAH is almost completely removed in one pass by filtration plus secretion through organic anion transporters, so its clearance approximates renal plasma flow; it is called effective because a small share of flow bypasses secreting tubules. Comparing any clearance with GFR shows whether the tubules added the substance (above GFR) or took it back (below GFR).

points: Proximal tubule reabsorbs about two thirds of filtered Na+ and water, nearly all glucose and amino acids, and most bicarbonate (Na+/H+ exchange).
Glucose rides SGLT2 with Na+; above a plasma level of about 200 mg/dL the carriers begin to saturate and glucose appears in urine.
Descending thin limb lets water out; ascending limbs are water impermeable.
Thick ascending limb: Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) reabsorbs about 25 percent of filtered Na+; K+ leaks back into the lumen.
That K+ back-leak makes the lumen positive, which pushes Mg2+ and Ca2+ between the cells into blood.
notes.why: Almost all proximal transport runs on the Na+ gradient made by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase: SGLT2 and the Na+/H+ exchanger use the inward flow of Na+ to carry glucose in and H+ out. Water follows the absorbed solute through aquaporin-1, so proximal reabsorption is isosmotic and tubular fluid stays at about 300 mOsm/kg. In the thick ascending limb, NKCC2 brings in Na+, K+, and 2 Cl-, and K+ leaks back out through ROMK channels, leaving the lumen positive. That voltage drives Ca2+ and Mg2+ between the cells, which is why loop diuretics waste calcium and magnesium as well as sodium.

points: Aldosterone (principal cells): more ENaC channels and Na+/K+-ATPase, so more Na+ reabsorbed and more K+ secreted.
ADH (V2 receptor, cAMP) inserts aquaporin-2 into the collecting duct luminal membrane so water follows the medullary gradient.
PTH increases Ca2+ reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule (and reduces phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule).
notes.why: These hormones act late in the nephron, where fine adjustments are made after bulk reabsorption is done. Aldosterone binds an intracellular mineralocorticoid receptor that increases transcription of ENaC and Na+/K+-ATPase; Na+ entry through ENaC makes the lumen negative, which drives K+ out through ROMK channels. ADH acts through the V2 receptor, Gs, cAMP, and protein kinase A, which moves aquaporin-2 from storage vesicles into the luminal membrane. PTH raises Ca2+ reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule and lowers phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule by removing Na+-phosphate cotransporters.

points: Thick ascending limb pumps NaCl out without water; the descending limb loses water; flow repeats this step along the loop (countercurrent multiplication).
The result is an interstitial gradient from about 300 mOsm/kg at the cortex to about 1200 mOsm/kg at the papilla.
Urea trapped in the inner medulla adds a large share of that gradient.
With ADH, collecting duct water leaves into the hypertonic medulla and urine reaches about 1200 mOsm/kg; without ADH, urine can be as dilute as about 50 mOsm/kg.
notes.why: The loop builds the gradient and the collecting duct uses it. The thick ascending limb can create only about a 200 mOsm/kg difference at any one level, but because fluid flows down one limb and back up the other, that small step is multiplied along the loop into a large gradient from cortex to papilla. In the inner medulla, ADH also opens urea transporters in the collecting duct, so urea moves into the interstitium and adds to the gradient. Without ADH action, as in central or nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, the collecting duct stays water-tight and the dilute fluid leaving the loop is excreted as dilute urine.

points: Water moves between ECF and ICF only when ECF osmolality changes.
Isotonic gain or loss changes only ECF volume.
Losing water (dehydration) or gaining salt raises osmolality and pulls water out of cells.
Gaining water or losing more salt than water lowers osmolality and swells cells.
notes.why: Water crosses cell membranes freely, so ICF and ECF always end at the same osmolality, and Na+ stays mostly outside cells, which makes it the main ECF osmole. Adding or losing isotonic fluid (saline infusion, hemorrhage) leaves ECF osmolality unchanged, so no water shifts and only ECF volume changes. Any change in ECF osmolality draws water into or out of cells until the two compartments match again, which is why hyponatremia swells brain cells (headache, confusion, seizures) and hypernatremia shrinks them.

points: Filling: sympathetic hypogastric nerve (about T11 to L2) relaxes the detrusor and contracts the internal sphincter; pudendal nerve (S2 to S4) keeps the external sphincter closed.
Voiding: stretch signals reach the pontine micturition center, which, when the cortex allows, fires pelvic parasympathetics (S2 to S4) to contract the detrusor and relaxes both sphincters.
Cord lesion above the sacral segments: reflex spastic bladder, small capacity, sudden emptying, and sphincter dyssynergia.
Lesion at the sacral cord or its roots: flaccid, overfilled bladder with overflow dribbling.
notes.why: Storage and voiding are opposite autonomic states, and the pontine micturition center switches between them. During storage, sympathetic beta-3 input relaxes the detrusor and alpha-1 input closes the internal sphincter, while pudendal fibers hold the external sphincter shut. When the cortex allows voiding, the pons turns off sympathetic and pudendal output and drives sacral parasympathetic fibers, whose acetylcholine acts on M3 receptors to contract the detrusor. A lesion above the sacral cord disconnects the pons, so the sacral reflex fires on its own and without sphincter coordination, while a sacral lesion destroys the reflex arc and leaves a flaccid bladder that overfills.

pitfalls: Creatinine clearance slightly overestimates true GFR because some creatinine is secreted.

summary: How the kidney keeps blood pH and blood pressure in range. Exam questions hand you a blood gas or electrolyte panel and ask you to name the disorder, judge compensation, find the cause from the anion gap, sort out the renal tubular acidoses, or explain hypertension with low potassium.

points: Proximal tubule secretes H+ through Na+/H+ exchange; H+ meets filtered HCO3- in the lumen.
Brush border carbonic anhydrase turns H2CO3 into CO2 and water, which enter the cell.
Inside, carbonic anhydrase makes H+ and HCO3- again; HCO3- goes to blood and H+ is recycled.
This reclaims about 80 percent of filtered HCO3- but adds no new base. Acetazolamide blocks it.
notes.why: Filtered HCO3- cannot cross the luminal membrane directly, so the tubule reclaims it as CO2. Secreted H+ combines with HCO3- in the lumen, brush border carbonic anhydrase splits the carbonic acid into CO2 and water, CO2 diffuses into the cell, and cytosolic carbonic anhydrase rebuilds H+ and HCO3-, which leaves through the basolateral membrane. The secreted H+ is used up in the lumen, so no acid is excreted and no new base is made. When this step fails (proximal, type 2 renal tubular acidosis), HCO3- is wasted until plasma HCO3- falls low enough that the smaller filtered load can be reclaimed.

points: Each H+ the kidney excretes with a buffer adds one new HCO3- to blood.
Titratable acid: secreted H+ binds filtered phosphate (HPO4 2- to H2PO4-).
Ammonium: proximal tubule breaks down glutamine into NH4+ and new HCO3-; NH4+ is excreted in urine.
Ammonium excretion rises a great deal in chronic acidosis and is the main adaptive response; hyperkalemia suppresses it.
Alpha-intercalated cells secrete H+ with an H+-ATPase; urine pH can fall to about 4.5.
notes.why: Metabolism makes nonvolatile acid every day that uses up HCO3-, so the kidney must make new HCO3- to replace it. Each H+ excreted on a urinary buffer leaves behind one new HCO3- made inside the cell, and buffers are essential because urine pH cannot fall below about 4.5. Phosphate buffering is limited by how much is filtered, while ammonium production from glutamine can rise several-fold in chronic acidosis, so ammonium is the main adaptive response. In distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis, alpha-intercalated cells cannot secrete enough H+, so urine pH stays above 5.5, and in type 4, hyperkalemia from low aldosterone effect suppresses ammonium production.

points: Normal: pH 7.35 to 7.45, PaCO2 35 to 45 mm Hg, HCO3- 22 to 28 mEq/L.
Step 1: acidemia or alkalemia. Step 2: if HCO3- moved in the same direction as pH, the primary problem is metabolic; if PaCO2 moved in the opposite direction, it is respiratory.
Metabolic acidosis: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 times HCO3- plus 8, plus or minus 2 (Winters formula).
Respiratory acidosis: HCO3- rises about 1 per 10 mm Hg PaCO2 acutely and about 3.5 per 10 after 3 to 5 days of renal compensation.
PaCO2 outside the expected range means a second, respiratory disorder is also present; compensation never brings pH all the way back.
notes.why: By the Henderson-Hasselbalch relation, pH depends on the ratio of HCO3- to PaCO2, so compensation moves the other value in the same direction to restore the ratio. The lungs compensate within minutes to hours, which is why the Winters formula can predict PaCO2 in metabolic acidosis. The kidneys need 3 to 5 days to raise HCO3- by making new bicarbonate, which explains the larger chronic respiratory compensation. Because compensation is driven by the pH change itself, it stops short of normal, so a normal pH with clearly abnormal PaCO2 and HCO3- signals two primary disorders.

points: Anion gap = Na+ minus (Cl- plus HCO3-); normal about 8 to 12 mEq/L.
High gap: an unmeasured acid has been added (lactate, ketoacids, uremic acids, formate from methanol, glycolate and oxalate from ethylene glycol, salicylate).
Normal gap (hyperchloremic): HCO3- was lost and replaced by Cl- (diarrhea, renal tubular acidosis, acetazolamide).
Low albumin lowers the gap and can hide a high gap acidosis.
notes.why: Electroneutrality requires total cations to equal total anions, so the anion gap simply measures unmeasured anions, mostly albumin. When an acid is added, its H+ is buffered by HCO3- while its anion stays in plasma, so HCO3- falls and the gap widens. When HCO3- is lost directly, as in diarrhea or renal tubular acidosis, the kidney retains Cl- to keep electroneutrality, so the gap stays normal and chloride rises. Each 1 g/dL drop in albumin lowers the expected gap by about 2.5 mEq/L, so hypoalbuminemia can hide a high gap acidosis.

points: Vomiting removes HCl, so HCO3- made by parietal cells stays in blood (hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis).
Volume loss raises angiotensin II and aldosterone; proximal tubules reclaim HCO3- avidly, and principal and intercalated cells trade Na+ for K+ and H+.
Result: hypokalemia from renal K+ loss, and acidic urine despite alkalemia (paradoxical aciduria).
Low Cl- delivery also blocks distal HCO3- excretion; urine Cl- is low, and saline corrects it.
notes.why: Each H+ secreted by parietal cells adds one HCO3- to the blood, which is normally balanced when pancreatic HCO3- neutralizes that acid in the duodenum; vomiting removes the acid, so the extra HCO3- stays. The kidney would normally excrete excess HCO3-, but volume loss, chloride loss, and hypokalemia keep it reclaiming: angiotensin II increases proximal Na+/H+ exchange, aldosterone drives distal Na+ reabsorption in exchange for K+ and H+, and low luminal Cl- limits HCO3- secretion by beta-intercalated cells. This is why the urine is acidic, most K+ is lost in urine, and saline corrects the alkalosis by restoring volume and chloride.

points: Renin release: low perfusion pressure at juxtaglomerular cells, low NaCl at the macula densa, beta-1 sympathetic stimulation.
Renin turns angiotensinogen into angiotensin I; ACE (mostly in lung endothelium) makes angiotensin II and breaks down bradykinin.
Angiotensin II: arteriolar constriction (efferent more than afferent), more proximal Na+ reabsorption, aldosterone release, ADH release, thirst.
Atrial natriuretic peptide from stretched atria does the opposite: natriuresis, raised GFR, vasodilation, less renin and aldosterone.
notes.why: Renin release is the rate-limiting step, and its three triggers all signal that effective circulating volume or pressure is low. Angiotensin II then restores volume and pressure at several levels: it constricts arterioles, holds GFR by favoring efferent tone, increases proximal Na+/H+ exchange, and stimulates aldosterone from the zona glomerulosa, ADH from the posterior pituitary, and thirst. ACE also breaks down bradykinin, so ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin, which explains their cough and angioedema. ANP signals volume excess: it raises GFR, inhibits renin and aldosterone, and reduces Na+ reabsorption in the collecting duct.

points: Pressure natriuresis: higher arterial pressure makes the kidney excrete more Na+ and water, shrinking ECF volume until pressure falls back.
Over days to weeks this kidney mechanism sets the long-term arterial pressure.
Primary hyperaldosteronism (adrenal adenoma or hyperplasia): hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, high aldosterone, low renin.
Edema is absent in primary hyperaldosteronism because pressure natriuresis and ANP limit volume gain (aldosterone escape).
notes.why: The baroreceptor reflex resets within days, so only the kidney can correct pressure indefinitely: while arterial pressure is above the set point, it excretes more salt and water than is taken in until volume and pressure fall. Sustained hypertension therefore requires the pressure natriuresis curve to shift to higher pressures, which excess aldosterone does by increasing distal Na+ reabsorption. The same aldosterone action drives K+ and H+ secretion, giving hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis, and the expanded volume suppresses renin. Volume rises only modestly because pressure natriuresis and ANP restore Na+ balance (aldosterone escape), so edema does not develop.

tricks.label: MUDPILES
tricks.text: High anion gap acidosis: Methanol, Uremia, Diabetic ketoacidosis, Propylene glycol, Iron tablets or isoniazid, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates.

tricks.label: HARDASS
tricks.text: Normal anion gap acidosis: Hyperalimentation, Addison disease, Renal tubular acidosis, Diarrhea, Acetazolamide, Spironolactone, Saline infusion.

tricks.label: Volume beats pH
tricks.text: When the body is short on volume, the kidney saves Na+ even if it must dump H+ and K+ to do it. That is why vomiting makes acid urine.

highYield: Ammonium excretion from glutamine is the kidney's main adaptable way to excrete acid.
Use Winters formula to check whether a metabolic acidosis has the right respiratory compensation.
Diarrhea and RTA give a normal anion gap; ketoacidosis, lactate, and toxic alcohols give a high gap.
Distal RTA: urine pH above 5.5, hypokalemia, calcium phosphate stones.
Type 4 RTA is the classic RTA with hyperkalemia; types 1 and 2 cause hypokalemia.
Vomiting gives hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with low urine Cl- and paradoxical aciduria.
Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole more and stimulates aldosterone, ADH, and thirst.
Hypertension, hypokalemia, and low renin point to primary hyperaldosteronism.
pitfalls: Reclaiming filtered HCO3- adds no new base; only excreting H+ as titratable acid or ammonium makes new HCO3-.
A normal pH with abnormal PaCO2 and HCO3- usually means a mixed disorder, since compensation does not fully normalize pH.
Proximal RTA can make an acid urine once serum HCO3- falls below the lowered threshold; urine pH alone does not rule it out.
Renovascular hypertension and primary hyperaldosteronism both raise aldosterone; renin is high in renovascular disease and low in primary disease.
Hypokalemia after vomiting comes mostly from renal K+ loss, since gastric fluid holds little K+.
